The pronoun in "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" may refer to "those who committed evil," meaning that their state in both times (life and death) is equal; or it may refer to the evildoers and the righteous together, meaning that the living and dying of the believers are equal in their humiliation before Allah and their lack of honour with Him. The wording wraps this meaning, and the listener's mind separates it, since Allah's distancing of making these like those was already mentioned. Abu al-Darda' said: people will be resurrected in the state in which they died. Mujahid said: the believer dies a believer and is raised a believer, and the disbeliever dies a disbeliever and is raised a disbeliever.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the apparent sense of this speech is the wording of the verse, but it appears to me that His saying "equal in their living and their dying" is included in the "good-doers" who "deny the evil," and this is a good possibility, though the first is also better. End of quote. He did not explain how the clause is connected to what precedes it so that it would fall under "the good-doers." Al-Zamakhshari said: the clause "equal in their living and their dying" is a substitute (badal) for the kaf (in "ka-alladhina"), because a clause may occur as a second object, so it has the status of a single noun. Do you not see that if you said: "that We make them equal in their living and their dying," it would be sound, just as you say: "I thought Zayd, his father is departing." End of quote. What al-Zamakhshari went to, substituting a clause for a single noun, was permitted by Abu al-Fath, and Ibn Malik preferred it, and cited examples for it, but in those examples the substitution is not definite.

One of our companions, the eminent scholar Diya' al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Ishbili, known as Ibn al-'Ilj, who lived in Yemen and composed works there, said in his book al-Basit fi al-Nahw: "It is not correct for it to be a clause governed by the first verb in the position of substitution, as in the case of a qualifier (na't), because it is estimated as a derived noun, not as a fixed noun, so it would be a substitute; thus there would be a combination of the permissibility of 'an' (the verbal clause) and a substitute, and because the substitute takes the first verb as its governor, so it could be a subject, and a clause cannot be in the position of a subject without a valid reason, since it is not implied. If it is not governed, can it be a clause? In my view it is not far-fetched to permit it, just as a clause is attached by conjunction to a clause, and an emphatic clause is emphasized by a verbal emphasis." End of quote.

It is clear from the speech of this imam that a clause cannot be a substitute for a single noun. As for al-Zamakhshari's permission of "that We make them equal in their living and their dying," it appears to me that it is not permitted, because it has the meaning of "making" (taSyir). It is not permitted to say: "I made Zayd, his father standing," nor "I made Zayd, his servant departing," because making involves a transfer from one entity to another, or from one attribute in an entity to another attribute in it. But that clause that follows a first object of "made" (Sayyara) makes the implied term a second object, and there is no transfer in it of what we mentioned, so it is not permitted. What appears to me is that if we hold that the clause is connected to what precedes it, the clause would be in the position of a state (hal), and the estimate is: "Did the disbelievers think that We would make them like the believers in a state where their living and dying are equal? They are not like that; rather they are divided," meaning a division in both states. This state would clarify what is ambiguous in the likeness indicated by the kaf, which is in the position of the second object.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read "sawa'an" with the accusative (nasb), and what follows it is in the nominative as the subject (fa'iliyyah), treating "sawa'" as "mustawiyan" (equal), as they say: "I passed by a man, equal, he and the nothing." As for the accusative of "sawa'," two possibilities are permitted: one is that it is accusative as a state (hal), and "ka-alladhina" is the second object; and the reverse. Al-A'mash read "sawa'an" with the accusative, and "mahyahum wa mamatahum" also with the accusative, and it is explained as "mahyahum wa mamatahum" being adverbs of time, and the governing word being either "an naj'alahum" or "sawa'an." It is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for the object of "naj'aluhum," and the second object is "sawa'an," (p-٤٨) meaning: that He makes their living and dying equal.

Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads "wa mamatahum" with the accusative makes "mahyahum wa mamatahum" adverbs, like "the arrival of the pilgrim" and "the rising of the star," meaning: equal in their living and in their dying, and the meaning is a denial that the evildoers and the good-doers be equal in life, or equal in death, because of the divergence of their states. His illustration with "khafuq al-najm" (the rising of the star) is not good, because khafuq is a verbal noun not of the form mafal, so it is in reality by omission of a modifier, meaning "the time of the rising of the star." Unlike mahya, mamat, and maqdim, which are used by convention as a verbal noun, a noun of time, and a noun of place. When they are used as a noun of place or a noun of time, it is not by omission of a modifier that this word takes the place of, because they are established for time and for place, just as they were established for the verbal noun, so they are shared among these three meanings. Unlike khafuq al-najm, which is established only for the verbal noun.

Ibn 'Atiyyah made an error in transmitting the Qur'anic readings, and he has some excuse, for he was not a grammarian. He said: Talhah ibn Musarrif and 'Isa, in one narration from him, read "sawa'un" with the nominative and "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" with the nominative... and Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and al-A'mash read "sawa'an" with the accusative, "mahyahum wa mamatahum" with the accusative. He explained each of the two readings according to what the science of grammatical parsing requires. Al-Muharrir's author followed him in this error, and he is excused, because he was copying from one book to another. The correct version is what we have clarified from the readings for those we mentioned.

From this verse may be derived the difference between the state of the believer who disobeys and the state of the obedient one, even though it is said about disbelievers, and it is called "the weeping of the worshippers." It is reported from Tamim al-Dari, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was praying one night by the Maqam, and when he reached this verse, he began to weep and repeated until morning: "Evil is their judgment." It is reported from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym that he would repeat it the whole night, and likewise al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad used to say to himself: "I wonder, to which of the two groups do you belong?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for its wording, it indicates that it is the earning of disbelief, by evidence of its being paralleled with belief; and it may be that the parallel is with "earning" and "doing righteous deeds," and belief would then be in both groups, and for this reason the fearful wept.

﴿Evil is their judgment﴾: it is like His saying: ﴿How evil is what they have sold﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:90], and its parsing was already discussed in Al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: here "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (maSdariyyah), and the estimate is: "Evil is the judgment of their judgment."

(bil-haqq): meaning that its creation is true and necessary because of the overflowing goods in it, and so that it may indicate Him by the indication of craftsmanship to the Craftsman.

﴿and so that﴾: is the "la" of purpose (lam kay), conjoined to "bil-haqq," because both the "ta" and the "lam" are for causation, so the creation was caused by recompense. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is conjoined to a hidden cause, estimated as: "so that by them He may show His power, and so that every soul may be recompensed." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be the "lam" of consequence (lam al-Sayrurah), meaning the matter turned out so that by it some were guided and others went astray, so that each one would be recompensed for his deed, and for what he earned of good or evil. End of quote.

(Have you seen...): the verse. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi. "Ara'ayta" here means "inform me," the first object is "him who took," and the second is omitted, estimated as "after the prayer, which is for the one who is guided," indicated by His saying afterward: ﴿who then will guide him after Allah﴾, meaning there is no one who can guide him after Allah has led him astray.

﴿who takes his own desire as his god﴾: meaning he is obedient to the desire of his own soul, following what it calls him to, so it is as if he worships it, as a man worships his god. Ibn Jubayr said: it is an indication of idols, since they used to worship the stones they desired. Qatadah said: he does not desire anything without mounting it, not fearing Allah; therefore it is said: desire is a worshipped god. Al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read "ilahata" with the feminine ta, as a substitute for the pronoun's hā'. And it is reported from al-A'raj that he read "alihata" in the plural. Ibn Khalawayh said: its meaning is that one of them desired a stone and worshipped it, then saw another and desired it, so he cast away the first, and likewise is His saying: ﴿his god, his desire﴾, etc. Even if it was revealed about the desire of disbelief, it encompasses all the desire of the commanding soul. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah did not mention desire except to condemn it. Wahb said: if you are in doubt between two matters, look at the one farther from your desire and go to it. Sahl al-Tustari said: your desire is your disease, and if you oppose it, it is your cure. In a hadith: "The one who is incapable is he who follows his soul's desires and wishes for Allah's forgiveness." Among the wisdom of poetry is the saying of 'Antarah, who was from the pre-Islamic period:

"I am a man of gentle disposition and nobility, who does not follow the stubborn soul in its desires."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 45, verses 18–26 (part 2 of 2):

Abu 'Imran Musa ibn 'Imran al-Ishbili al-Zahid, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"So oppose her desires and disobey her, for whoever obeys the desire of his soul / will be pulled by it toward the worst of destinations.
And whoever obeys the stubborn soul, it will drive him down and hurl him into a fall, what a terrible fall!"

﴿And Allah misguided him knowingly﴾: meaning, from Allah, the Exalted, by His prior decree; or "knowingly" refers to this misguided person's own knowledge that the truth is the religion, yet he turns away from it out of obstinacy. This is like His saying: ﴿and they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He turned him away from guidance and divine kindness (luṭf), and abandoned him knowingly, aware that this would not benefit him, and that he is one for whom there is no kindness; or [it means] with His knowledge of the ways of guidance and His encompassing of the kinds of kindness that bring about and draw near [to guidance]." End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-I'tizal, the Mu'tazilite school).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ghishawatan﴾ with a kasra on the ghayn. 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] and al-A'mash read it with a fatha, and this is the dialect of Rabi'a. Al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, and also 'Abdullah read it with a damma, which is the dialect of 'Ukl. Al-A'mash, Talha, Abu Hanifa, Mas'ud ibn Salih, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿ghashwatan﴾ with a fatha on the ghayn and a sukun on the shin. Ibn Musarrif and also al-A'mash read it likewise, except that both of them read the ghayn with a kasra. The explanation of the two sentences has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The majority read ﴿tadhakkarun﴾ with a shadda on the dhal. Al-Jahdari reads it without the shadda, and al-A'mash reads it with two taʼs (tatadhakkarun).

﴿And they said: "There is nothing but our life of this world"﴾ [Al-An'am: 29]: this is the statement of some of the Quraysh, denying resurrection. The apparent meaning of their saying "We die and we live" is a judgment on the species as a whole, without considering order of precedence, i.e., some die and some live. And the meaning of "death" is the separation of the soul from the body. It has been said that there is a transposition in the speech, i.e., "We live and we die." It has also been said that "we die" is an expression for their not having existed, and "we live" means at the time of our existence; this is close to the first view before it. In these two statements there is no mention of death in the sense of the separation of the soul. It has also been said: "The fathers die and the sons live." Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿wanahya﴾ with a damma on the nun.

﴿And nothing destroys us except time (al-dahr)﴾: that is, the long passage of time, because calamities are equally attributed to it. This is if those who say this acknowledged Allah, and they attributed calamities to time out of their ignorance that these are decreed by Allah. But if they did not know Allah nor affirm Him, and they were the Dahriyya (materialist deniers who attributed events to time), then they attributed that to time. 'Abdullah read ﴿illa dahrun﴾, and its interpretation is: "except a passing age." They used to attribute every occurrence to time, and their poetry speaks of complaints against time, to the point that this is found in the poetry of Muslims too. Ibn Duraid said in his maqsura (a rhyming poem with a long vowel):

"O time, if you are not going to grant me a reprieve, then take your time,
for your delaying and your reproach are equal."

﴿Their argument was not⦆ (mā kāna ḥujjatahum): it is not an argument in reality. That is, [it is] their argument in their own eyes, or because they presented it as an argument does one who argues present his proof, and they brought it in the manner of one who argues, so it was called an argument by way of mockery. Or it is like their saying:

"Their greeting among themselves is a painful blow,"

meaning: their argument was nothing but what is not an argument. The intended meaning is the negation that they have any argument at all. The majority read ﴿ḥujjatahum﴾ in the accusative (naṣb). Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Ibn 'Amir (as reported by 'Abd al-Hamid), and 'Asim (as reported by Harun and Husayn, from Abu Bakr from him) read ﴿ḥujjatuhum﴾ in the nominative, meaning "what their argument is." This is because idha (when) denotes the future, and it differs from conditional particles in that when its response is negated by ma, the fa' (then) is not used, unlike with conditional particles, where the fa' is required. You say: "If you visit us, you have not been harsh to us," meaning "then you will not be harsh to us." That the response is negated by ma is evidence for what we have chosen, namely that the response of idha does not govern it, because what follows the negative ma does not govern what precedes it.

﴿Bring (ui'tu)﴾: it appears that this is an address to the Messenger and the believers, since they are the ones who say his statement; or it is an address to him and to the one who brought resurrection, who are the prophets, and the address takes precedence over the third-person form. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "[Bring] is addressed to him directly. The intended meaning is: he, his God, and the intermediary angel which he mentioned are with them; so there came from that a clause in which it was said 'bring,' and [they were addressed] 'if you are truthful.'" End of quote.

When they acknowledged that nothing destroys them except time, and that they argued for denying resurrection with something that has no proof for them, namely asking for the revival of their fathers, Allah the Exalted responded to them that it is He who gives life and He who causes death, not time. He added to that a verse that encompasses the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. Acknowledging this is obligatory for them if they are fair-minded. And whoever is capable of this is capable of bringing back their fathers. (p. 50)

(p-٤٦)﴿Then We placed you on a path of the matter, so follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they will not avail you anything against Allah. And indeed, the wrongdoers are allies of one another, while Allah is the Ally of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿This is insight for mankind, and guidance and mercy for a people who are certain.﴾ ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will treat them as those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is their judgment.﴾ ﴿And Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Have you seen him who takes his own desire as his god, and Allah has led him astray knowingly, and has sealed his hearing and his heart, and placed a covering over his sight? Who then will guide him after Allah? Will you not take heed?﴾ ﴿And they say: "There is nothing but our life of this world. We die and we live, and only time destroys us." They have no knowledge of that; they only conjecture.﴾ ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, their argument is only that they say: "Bring our fathers, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Say: "Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then will gather you to the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt," but most people do not know.﴾

When He mentioned His blessing upon the Children of Israel and their disagreement after that, He mentioned the state of His Prophet, peace be upon him, and the favour of choosing him, saying: ﴿Then We placed you on a path of the matter, so follow it, and do not follow the desires...﴾. Qatadah said: the sharI'ah (path, law) is the command, the prohibition, the limits and the obligations. Muqatil said: it is the clear proof, because it is a path to the truth. Al-Kalbi said: it is the sunnah, because he followed the way of the prophets before him. Ibn Zayd said: it is the religion, because it is a path to salvation. In the speech of the Arabs, the sharI'ah is the place where people come down to the rivers and waters. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And among the watering places of Jilan is a hunter, ragged of garments, obscure of person, slender-bodied."

So the sharI'ah of the religion, from this meaning, is that to which people come for the command of Allah, His mercy and nearness to Him, from the matters of the religion of Allah which He sent to His servants in past times. Or it may be a verbal noun (maSdar) of "command," meaning from the command and the prohibition, and the prohibition was called a command.

﴿the desires of those who do not know﴾: it was said they are the ignorant of Qurayzah and al-Nadir. It was also said they are the leaders of Quraysh, when they said: "Return to the religion of your fathers."

﴿This is insight﴾: that is, this Qur'an, (the particle) "ha-dha" being demonstrative, is from the landmarks of the religion, insight for hearts, just as it was made a spirit and life. It was also read as "hadhi," meaning these verses.

﴿Or do they think﴾: "am" here is disjunctive (munqaTi'ah), estimated as "bal" with the interrogative hamza, and it is an interrogation of denial (istifham inkar). Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali, Hamzah, 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, and concerning 'Utbah, Shaybah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. They said to the believers: "By Allah, you are not upon anything. And even if what you say is true, our state is better than yours in the Hereafter, just as it is better in this world." (Ijtarahu) means they earned; "the evil deeds" here means the evil deeds of disbelief. (Najʿaluhum) means we make them; the second object is "ka-alladhina," and with it the meaning is complete. The majority read "sawa'" with a nominative (raf') and "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" also with a nominative, and they parsed "sawa'" as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being what follows it. There is no justification for beginning with it, rather it is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and what follows it is the subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). The clause is a new predicate (khabar mustanaf). The pronoun in "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" may refer to "those who committed evil," meaning that their state in both times (life and death) is equal; or it may refer to the evildoers and the righteous together, meaning that the living and dying of the believers are equal in their humiliation before Allah and their lack of honour with Him. The wording wraps this meaning, and the listener's mind separates it, since Allah's distancing of making these like those was already mentioned. Abu al-Darda' said: people will be resurrected in the state in which they died. Mujahid said: the believer dies a believer and is raised a believer, and the disbeliever dies a disbeliever and is raised a disbeliever.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the apparent sense of this speech is the wording of the verse, but it appears to me that His saying "equal in their living and their dying" is included in the "good-doers" who "deny the evil," and this is a good possibility, though the first is also better. End of quote. He did not explain how the clause is connected to what precedes it so that it would fall under "the good-doers." Al-Zamakhshari said: the clause "equal in their living and their dying" is a substitute (badal) for the kaf (in "ka-alladhina"), because a clause may occur as a second object, so it has the status of a single noun. Do you not see that if you said: "that We make them equal in their living and their dying," it would be sound, just as you say: "I thought Zayd, his father is departing." End of quote. What al-Zamakhshari went to, substituting a clause for a single noun, was permitted by Abu al-Fath, and Ibn Malik preferred it, and cited examples for it, but in those examples the substitution is not definite.

One of our companions, the eminent scholar Diya' al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Ishbili, known as Ibn al-'Ilj, who lived in Yemen and composed works there, said in his book al-Basit fi al-Nahw: "It is not correct for it to be a clause governed by the first verb in the position of substitution, as in the case of a qualifier (na't), because it is estimated as a derived noun, not as a fixed noun, so it would be a substitute; thus there would be a combination of the permissibility of 'an' (the verbal clause) and a substitute, and because the substitute takes the first verb as its governor, so it could be a subject, and a clause cannot be in the position of a subject without a valid reason, since it is not implied. If it is not governed, can it be a clause? In my view it is not far-fetched to permit it, just as a clause is attached by conjunction to a clause, and an emphatic clause is emphasized by a verbal emphasis." End of quote.

It is clear from the speech of this imam that a clause cannot be a substitute for a single noun. As for al-Zamakhshari's permission of "that We make them equal in their living and their dying," it appears to me that it is not permitted, because it has the meaning of "making" (taSyir). It is not permitted to say: "I made Zayd, his father standing," nor "I made Zayd, his servant departing," because making involves a transfer from one entity to another, or from one attribute in an entity to another attribute in it. But that clause that follows a first object of "made" (Sayyara) makes the implied term a second object, and there is no transfer in it of what we mentioned, so it is not permitted. What appears to me is that if we hold that the clause is connected to what precedes it, the clause would be in the position of a state (hal), and the estimate is: "Did the disbelievers think that We would make them like the believers in a state where their living and dying are equal? They are not like that; rather they are divided," meaning a division in both states. This state would clarify what is ambiguous in the likeness indicated by the kaf, which is in the position of the second object.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read "sawa'an" with the accusative (nasb), and what follows it is in the nominative as the subject (fa'iliyyah), treating "sawa'" as "mustawiyan" (equal), as they say: "I passed by a man, equal, he and the nothing." As for the accusative of "sawa'," two possibilities are permitted: one is that it is accusative as a state (hal), and "ka-alladhina" is the second object; and the reverse. Al-A'mash read "sawa'an" with the accusative, and "mahyahum wa mamatahum" also with the accusative, and it is explained as "mahyahum wa mamatahum" being adverbs of time, and the governing word being either "an naj'alahum" or "sawa'an." It is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for the object of "naj'aluhum," and the second object is "sawa'an," (p-٤٨) meaning: that He makes their living and dying equal.

Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads "wa mamatahum" with the accusative makes "mahyahum wa mamatahum" adverbs, like "the arrival of the pilgrim" and "the rising of the star," meaning: equal in their living and in their dying, and the meaning is a denial that the evildoers and the good-doers be equal in life, or equal in death, because of the divergence of their states. His illustration with "khafuq al-najm" (the rising of the star) is not good, because khafuq is a verbal noun not of the form mafal, so it is in reality by omission of a modifier, meaning "the time of the rising of the star." Unlike mahya, mamat, and maqdim, which are used by convention as a verbal noun, a noun of time, and a noun of place. When they are used as a noun of place or a noun of time, it is not by omission of a modifier that this word takes the place of, because they are established for time and for place, just as they were established for the verbal noun, so they are shared among these three meanings. Unlike khafuq al-najm, which is established only for the verbal noun.

Ibn 'Atiyyah made an error in transmitting the Qur'anic readings, and he has some excuse, for he was not a grammarian. He said: Talhah ibn Musarrif and 'Isa, in one narration from him, read "sawa'un" with the nominative and "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" with the nominative... and Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and al-A'mash read "sawa'an" with the accusative, "mahyahum wa mamatahum" with the accusative. He explained each of the two readings according to what the science of grammatical parsing requires. Al-Muharrir's author followed him in this error, and he is excused, because he was copying from one book to another. The correct version is what we have clarified from the readings for those we mentioned.

From this verse may be derived the difference between the state of the believer who disobeys and the state of the obedient one, even though it is said about disbelievers, and it is called "the weeping of the worshippers." It is reported from Tamim al-Dari, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was praying one night by the Maqam, and when he reached this verse, he began to weep and repeated until morning: "Evil is their judgment." It is reported from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym that he would repeat it the whole night, and likewise al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad used to say to himself: "I wonder, to which of the two groups do you belong?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for its wording, it indicates that it is the earning of disbelief, by evidence of its being paralleled with belief; and it may be that the parallel is with "earning" and "doing righteous deeds," and belief would then be in both groups, and for this reason the fearful wept.

﴿Evil is their judgment﴾: it is like His saying: ﴿How evil is what they have sold﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:90], and its parsing was already discussed in Al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: here "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (maSdariyyah), and the estimate is: "Evil is the judgment of their judgment."

(bil-haqq): meaning that its creation is true and necessary because of the overflowing goods in it, and so that it may indicate Him by the indication of craftsmanship to the Craftsman.

﴿and so that﴾: is the "la" of purpose (lam kay), conjoined to "bil-haqq," because both the "ta" and the "lam" are for causation, so the creation was caused by recompense. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is conjoined to a hidden cause, estimated as: "so that by them He may show His power, and so that every soul may be recompensed." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be the "lam" of consequence (lam al-Sayrurah), meaning the matter turned out so that by it some were guided and others went astray, so that each one would be recompensed for his deed, and for what he earned of good or evil. End of quote.

(Have you seen...): the verse. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi. "Ara'ayta" here means "inform me," the first object is "him who took," and the second is omitted, estimated as "after the prayer, which is for the one who is guided," indicated by His saying afterward: ﴿who then will guide him after Allah﴾, meaning there is no one who can guide him after Allah has led him astray.

﴿who takes his own desire as his god﴾: meaning he is obedient to the desire of his own soul, following what it calls him to, so it is as if he worships it, as a man worships his god. Ibn Jubayr said: it is an indication of idols, since they used to worship the stones they desired. Qatadah said: he does not desire anything without mounting it, not fearing Allah; therefore it is said: desire is a worshipped god. Al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read "ilahata" with the feminine ta, as a substitute for the pronoun's hā'. And it is reported from al-A'raj that he read "alihata" in the plural. Ibn Khalawayh said: its meaning is that one of them desired a stone and worshipped it, then saw another and desired it, so he cast away the first, and likewise is His saying: ﴿his god, his desire﴾, etc. Even if it was revealed about the desire of disbelief, it encompasses all the desire of the commanding soul. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah did not mention desire except to condemn it. Wahb said: if you are in doubt between two matters, look at the one farther from your desire and go to it. Sahl al-Tustari said: your desire is your disease, and if you oppose it, it is your cure. In a hadith: "The one who is incapable is he who follows his soul's desires and wishes for Allah's forgiveness." Among the wisdom of poetry is the saying of 'Antarah, who was from the pre-Islamic period:

"I am a man of gentle disposition and nobility, who does not follow the stubborn soul in its desires."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 45, verses 18–26 (part 2 of 2):

Abu 'Imran Musa ibn 'Imran al-Ishbili al-Zahid, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"So oppose her desires and disobey her, for whoever obeys the desire of his soul / will be pulled by it toward the worst of destinations.
And whoever obeys the stubborn soul, it will drive him down and hurl him into a fall, what a terrible fall!"

﴿And Allah misguided him knowingly﴾: meaning, from Allah, the Exalted, by His prior decree; or "knowingly" refers to this misguided person's own knowledge that the truth is the religion, yet he turns away from it out of obstinacy. This is like His saying: ﴿and they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [An-Naml: 14]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He turned him away from guidance and divine kindness (luṭf), and abandoned him knowingly, aware that this would not benefit him, and that he is one for whom there is no kindness; or [it means] with His knowledge of the ways of guidance and His encompassing of the kinds of kindness that bring about and draw near [to guidance]." End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-I'tizal, the Mu'tazilite school).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ghishawatan﴾ with a kasra on the ghayn. 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] and al-A'mash read it with a fatha, and this is the dialect of Rabi'a. Al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, and also 'Abdullah read it with a damma, which is the dialect of 'Ukl. Al-A'mash, Talha, Abu Hanifa, Mas'ud ibn Salih, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿ghashwatan﴾ with a fatha on the ghayn and a sukun on the shin. Ibn Musarrif and also al-A'mash read it likewise, except that both of them read the ghayn with a kasra. The explanation of the two sentences has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The majority read ﴿tadhakkarun﴾ with a shadda on the dhal. Al-Jahdari reads it without the shadda, and al-A'mash reads it with two taʼs (tatadhakkarun).

﴿And they said: "There is nothing but our life of this world"﴾ [Al-An'am: 29]: this is the statement of some of the Quraysh, denying resurrection. The apparent meaning of their saying "We die and we live" is a judgment on the species as a whole, without considering order of precedence, i.e., some die and some live. And the meaning of "death" is the separation of the soul from the body. It has been said that there is a transposition in the speech, i.e., "We live and we die." It has also been said that "we die" is an expression for their not having existed, and "we live" means at the time of our existence; this is close to the first view before it. In these two statements there is no mention of death in the sense of the separation of the soul. It has also been said: "The fathers die and the sons live." Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿wanahya﴾ with a damma on the nun.

﴿And nothing destroys us except time (al-dahr)﴾: that is, the long passage of time, because calamities are equally attributed to it. This is if those who say this acknowledged Allah, and they attributed calamities to time out of their ignorance that these are decreed by Allah. But if they did not know Allah nor affirm Him, and they were the Dahriyya (materialist deniers who attributed events to time), then they attributed that to time. 'Abdullah read ﴿illa dahrun﴾, and its interpretation is: "except a passing age." They used to attribute every occurrence to time, and their poetry speaks of complaints against time, to the point that this is found in the poetry of Muslims too. Ibn Duraid said in his maqsura (a rhyming poem with a long vowel):

"O time, if you are not going to grant me a reprieve, then take your time,
for your delaying and your reproach are equal."

﴿Their argument was not⦆ (mā kāna ḥujjatahum): it is not an argument in reality. That is, [it is] their argument in their own eyes, or because they presented it as an argument does one who argues present his proof, and they brought it in the manner of one who argues, so it was called an argument by way of mockery. Or it is like their saying:

"Their greeting among themselves is a painful blow,"

meaning: their argument was nothing but what is not an argument. The intended meaning is the negation that they have any argument at all. The majority read ﴿ḥujjatahum﴾ in the accusative (naṣb). Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Ibn 'Amir (as reported by 'Abd al-Hamid), and 'Asim (as reported by Harun and Husayn, from Abu Bakr from him) read ﴿ḥujjatuhum﴾ in the nominative, meaning "what their argument is." This is because idha (when) denotes the future, and it differs from conditional particles in that when its response is negated by ma, the fa' (then) is not used, unlike with conditional particles, where the fa' is required. You say: "If you visit us, you have not been harsh to us," meaning "then you will not be harsh to us." That the response is negated by ma is evidence for what we have chosen, namely that the response of idha does not govern it, because what follows the negative ma does not govern what precedes it.

﴿Bring (ui'tu)﴾: it appears that this is an address to the Messenger and the believers, since they are the ones who say his statement; or it is an address to him and to the one who brought resurrection, who are the prophets, and the address takes precedence over the third-person form. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "[Bring] is addressed to him directly. The intended meaning is: he, his God, and the intermediary angel which he mentioned are with them; so there came from that a clause in which it was said 'bring,' and [they were addressed] 'if you are truthful.'" End of quote.

When they acknowledged that nothing destroys them except time, and that they argued for denying resurrection with something that has no proof for them, namely asking for the revival of their fathers, Allah the Exalted responded to them that it is He who gives life and He who causes death, not time. He added to that a verse that encompasses the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. Acknowledging this is obligatory for them if they are fair-minded. And whoever is capable of this is capable of bringing back their fathers. (p. 50)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 45, verses 27–37:**

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. On the Day the Hour is established, on that Day the falsifiers will be lost.﴾ ﴿And you will see every community kneeling. Every community will be called to its record: "Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿This is Our Record, which speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We used to have it copied from what you used to do.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, their Lord will admit them into His mercy. That is the manifest triumph.﴾ ﴿And as for those who disbelieved: "Were My verses not recited to you? But you were arrogant, and you were a criminal people."﴾ ﴿And when it was said, "Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and the Hour, there is no doubt about it," you said, "We do not know what the Hour is. We only assume an assumption, and we are not certain."﴾ ﴿And the evils of what they had done will appear to them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾ ﴿And it will be said, "Today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this your Day. Your refuge is the Fire, and you have no helpers."﴾ ﴿That is because you took the verses of Allah in jest, and the worldly life deceived you." So today they will not be taken out of it, nor will they be allowed to make amends.﴾ ﴿So to Allah belongs all praise, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿And His is the majesty in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The element that governs (ويَوْمَ تَقُومُ) is ﴿يَخْسَرُ﴾ ("will be lost"). (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is a substitute (badal, a noun in apposition) for (يَوْمٍ). This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and Ibn Atiyya related it from a group of scholars. The nunation (تَنْوِينُ) in (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is the compensatory nunation (tanwin al-iwad, the nunation that stands in place of a omitted clause). No clause preceded it except His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ تَقُومُ السّاعَةُ﴾, so the estimated meaning becomes: "and on the Day the Hour is established, a day when the Hour is established, when the Hour is established, will be lost." There is no added benefit in the phrase "a day when the Hour is established," because that is already understood from "and on the Day the Hour is established." If it is an emphatic substitute (badal tawkidi, a substitute for emphasis), which is rare, then this is permissible; otherwise it cannot be a substitute. A group said that the governing element for (ويَوْمَ تَقُومُ) is what the dominion implies. They said: the Day of Resurrection is a third state, which is neither the heavens nor the earth, since those change. So it is as if He said: "To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth," and the dominion on the Day of Resurrection [is His], and He omitted it because what precedes it indicates it. (ويَوْمَئِذٍ) [al-Rum: 4] is in the accusative governed by ﴿يَخْسَرُ﴾, and this is a sentence that begins anew (isti'naf), though it has a connection to what precedes it through the compensatory nunation. (المُبْطِلُونَ) means those who enter into falsehood (al-batil).

﴿جاثِيَةً﴾ (kneeling) means sitting on the knees, alert and tense, which is the posture of a sinner who is afraid. It was also read as (جاذِيَةً) with a dhal, and (al-jadhw) is more tense in its readiness than (al-jathw), because the one who (jadhi) is the one who sits on the tips of his toes. From Ibn Abbas: "jathiyatan": gathered together. From Qatada: in groups, from (al-juthwa), which means a group, and its plural is (juthiyy). The poet said:

*You see two heaps of earth upon them, with solid slabs of piled stone over them.*

From Mawraj al-Sadusi: "jathiyatan" means submissive, in the dialect of Quraysh. From Ikrima: "jathiyatan" means distinguished. Ya'qub read ﴿كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ تُدْعى﴾ with (كُلَّ أُمَّةٍ) in the accusative, as a substitute of an indefinite qualified noun from an indefinite noun. The apparent meaning is the generality of every community, believers and disbelievers alike. Al-Dahhak said: this is at the time of reckoning. Yahya ibn Salam said: this is specific to the disbelievers, who are called to their book revealed to them, and they are judged by it, whether it agreed with it or opposed it; or [it refers to] what the recording angels wrote, which is the pages of their deeds; or the Preserved Tablet; or the meaning is "to what has been decreed for them," that is, to their reckoning. These are opinions. He used the singular (كِتابَها) relying on the generic noun, as in His saying ﴿ووُضِعَ الكِتابُ﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and ﴿اليَوْمَ تُجْزَوْنَ﴾ and ﴿هَذا كِتابُنا﴾. It is the one to which every community was called. Its attribution to Him, exalted is He, is correct because He is its owner and the one who commanded its writing; and its attribution to them is correct because their deeds are recorded in it. Attribution (al-idafa) may occur with the slightest connection, so its attribution to them and to Him, exalted is He, is valid.

﴿يَنْطِقُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ means it bears witness against you with truth, without addition or reduction.

﴿إنّا كُنّا نَسْتَنْسِخُ﴾: that is, the angels; i.e., We cause them to copy (تَنْسِخُ), that is, to write. The essential meaning of copying (al-naskh) is transferring a script from an original in which it is arranged, so the deeds of the servants are as if they were the original. Al-Hasan said: it is the writing of the guardian angels upon the children of Adam. From Ibn Abbas: Allah causes the guardian angels to copy from the Preserved Tablet everything that the servants do, and then they keep it with them, so the deeds of the servants come in accordance with that. This is also far-fetched, for that is the (istinsakh, copying). Ibn Abbas used to say: "Are you not Arabs? Does copying happen except from an original?"

Then he explained the state of the believer: that He admits him into His mercy, which is the reward prepared for him, and that this is the attainment of the desired goal. And he explained the state of the disbeliever: that he is rebuked and it is said to him, ﴿أفَلَمْ تَكُنْ آياتِي تُتْلى عَلَيْكم فاسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ﴾, meaning you were arrogant toward following them and believing in them, and you were people of crimes. The fa' in (أفَلَمْ) is intended to indicate sequence [or a conjunction with what precedes], and the interrogative hamza was placed first because the interrogative has the front position of the sentence. The estimated meaning is: "Then it is said to him, 'Did not...'" Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "Did My messengers not come to you? Then My verses were not recited to you," so the conjoined element has been omitted. End of quote. The discussion with him has already preceded regarding his claim that between the fa' and the waw, when the interrogative hamza precedes it, there is an omitted conjoined element; we have refuted that claim.

Al-A'raj and Amr ibn Fa'id read (وإذا قِيلَ أنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ) with the hamza opened (anna), and this is according to the dialect of Sulaym. The majority read (inna) with the hamza kasra'd. The majority read (والسّاعَةُ) with the nominative, as a new sentence (ibtida'). Whoever claims that the subject of (inna) has a position (mawdi') allowed conjoining to it here, or claims that (inna) and its subject together have a position, allowing conjoining to it, and conjoining to the position of (inna) and its subject here. Abu Ali said: he mentioned this in al-Hujja, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, saying: "And with the nominative, conjoined to the position of inna and its subject." The correct view is prohibition. Hamza read it with the accusative, conjoined to (الله), and this is related from al-A'mash, Abu Amr, Isa, Abu Haywa, al-Absi, and al-Mufaddal.

﴿إنْ نَظُنُّ إلّا ظَنًّا﴾: you say "I struck a striking" (darabtu darban); if you negate it, you do not introduce (illa), because the emphatic verbal noun (al-masdar al-mu'akkad) is not isolated (yufarragh) for it. So you do not say, "I did not strike except a striking," or "I did not stand except a standing." As for the verse, it is interpreted by omitting the descriptor of the verbal noun until it becomes restrictive (mukhtassan), not emphatic. Its estimated meaning is: "except an assumption that is weak." Or [it is interpreted] by implying in "nazunnu" the meaning of "na'taqidu" (we believe), with "zannan" as a direct object. Some have interpreted it as placing "illa" in a position other than its proper place, saying the estimated meaning is: "we are not except that we assume an assumption." This is related from al-Mubarrad. Its parallel is what Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' and Sibawayh related from the speech of the Arabs:

*Perfume is nothing but musk.*

Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "Perfume is nothing but musk [i.e., musk is the perfume]." End of quote. This estimate was needed because "musk" is nominative after (illa), while if you say (ma kana Zaydun illa fadilan), you put it in the accusative. When what appears after (illa) is apparently the predicate of (laysa), he needed to shift (illa) from its place, and make in (laysa) a pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and put the nominative on (illa al-tibu al-misk) as subject and predicate, so that it becomes like something pronounced, as in: (ma kana illa Zaydun qa'imun). Al-Mubarrad did not know that in this kind of construction the Tamim tribe treated (laysa) like (ma), so they only used it while it remained in place, and it was not governing. There is no Hijazi in the land who does not put the accusative in such a construction as "laysa al-tibu illa al-misk," and no Tamimi who does not put the nominative. There is an anecdote concerning this that passed between Isa ibn Umar and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala', which we have mentioned in what we wrote on the science of grammar. A parallel to ﴿إنْ نَظُنُّ إلّا ظَنًّا﴾ (p-52) is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Grey hair bore its burdens upon him, and grey hair did not deceive him except with a deception*, that is, a clear deception.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of "nazunnu illa zannan"? I say: its origin is "nazunnu zannan," and its meaning is affirming the assumption together with negating anything other than it; and [the verse] negated what was other than the assumption, as emphasis, by His saying "and we are not certain." End of quote. This speech comes from one who has no awareness of the grammatical rule, that the restrictive construction (tafrigh) occurs with all the operands, such as subject, object, and others, except the emphatic verbal noun, for it does not occur with it. Some estimated it as: "nazunnu illa anna-kum tazunnuna zannan" (we only assume that you assume an assumption). He said: this estimate is needed because it is not permissible in speech to say, "ma darabtu illa darban." He was guided to this grammatical rule but erred in the analysis. This is related from al-Mubarrad, and perhaps it is not sound. Their saying "nazunnu" is evidence that the disbelievers had reported that they assumed resurrection to occur, and their saying before His saying "in hiya illa hayatuna al-dunya" (there is nothing but our worldly life) indicates that they deny resurrection. So they are, and Allah knows best, two groups, or they were confused: at times they denied, and at times they assumed, and they said ﴿إنْ نَظُنُّ إلّا ظَنًّا﴾ as a form of mockery.

﴿وبَدا لَهم سَيِّئاتُ ما عَمِلُوا﴾: that is, the ugly consequences of their deeds, or the punishments of their evil deeds. "Evil" (sayyi'at) was applied to the punishment, as He said: ﴿وجَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُها﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

﴿وحاقَ بِهِمْ﴾ means encompassed them. (Haqa) is used only for what is disliked.

﴿نَنْساكُمْ﴾: We leave you in the punishment, or We make you like a forgotten thing, cast aside, not cared for.

﴿كَما نَسِيتُمْ لِقاءَ يَوْمِكُمْ﴾: that is, the meeting with Allah's recompense for your deeds, which you did not bring to mind after you had been reminded of it and had been warned of its occurrence. He attributed "meeting" to "day" in a broad sense, like His saying ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ والنَّهارِ﴾ [Saba': 33]. The majority read (لا يُخْرَجُونَ) in the passive. Al-Hasan, Ibn Thabit, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it in the active. (مِنها) means from the Fire.

﴿ولا هم يُسْتَعْتَبُونَ﴾ means they are not asked to return to righteous deeds. The discussion of (al-isti'tab, seeking to make amends) has already preceded. The majority read (رَبِّ) in the genitive in all three instances as an adjective, while Ibn Muhaysin read it in the nominative in both, as if supplying "huwa" (He).
